title: House committee launches investigation into Republican lawmaker amid domestic abuse allegations – as it happened
summary: Max Miller says he has ‘nothing to hide’ amid domestic abuse allegations made against him by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of Republican Ohio senator Bernie Moreno
body: Thanks for following our live coverage of the second Trump administration. Stay tuned to our blog dedicated to the US midterm primary elections, where we’ll be watching the latest developments in Michigan, Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. Here are the highlights for today: The US Senate judiciary committee voted along party lines to advance Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general after he confirmed in writing that a planned $1.8bn slush fund for Donald Trump’s allies was dead. Experts say, however, that Trump could easily reverse the deal. More here. Max Miller, a US Republican representative from Ohio, is facing a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. The House ethics committee announced it will launch an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct” after the embattled Republican said he had “nothing to hide” and welcomed the investigation. More here. Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. More here. An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. More here. A New York law banning US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from wearing face coverings and requiring that they wear visible identification has been put on hold by a federal judge. But a state law prohibiting cooperation between local police departments and ICE has been allowed to stand. More here. Answering whether the release of a link containing private photographs of his daughter was reckless, Max Miller said that the incident “is being taken very much out of context.” “This is once again a very salacious headline,” Miller said. “I didn’t do this. My attorney took full responsibility. I believe that it’s awful. There was never any intent to do that.” Miller was also pressed by Jake Tapper on whether he believed the three women accusing him of violent behavior were all lying. “For no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations and be pushed out of a seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community,” Miller said. “I’ve been a good legislator. All they’re trying to do is create rumor mills without evidence.” Asked whether he would consider dropping out of the race for the sake of his own mental health and his daughter’s well-being, Miller said he is “never going to give up.” “My daughter is going to grow up one day, and she’s going to see all of this, and she’s not going to see that her father caved to political and social media pressures,” Miller said. In an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper, embattled Ohio representative Max Miller rejected claims from Senator Bernie Moreno (his former father-in-law) that Miller withheld his daughter’s favorite stuffed toy during a custody exchange. “I would agree that if that were true, that would be incredibly disturbing,” Miller told Tapper on Tuesday. “This is nothing more than an individual who’s being politically vindictive.” Moreno has called for Miller to withdraw from his re-election bid amid allegations of domestic abuse and seek professional help. On Tuesday, he described the experience as “truly the seventh level of hell” for his family. An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location. In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award. “Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS. The Associated Press is reporting that the Trump administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the United States in retaliation for Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit the country ahead of upcoming elections as well as Brazil’s stalling on approving President Donald Trump’s nominee to be ambassador in Brazil. The state department said the decision was a reciprocal response to Brazil’s move and officials said the step had been delayed several times to give Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva room to back down, something he did not do. Officials said it could be quickly reversed if Brazil takes appropriate action and accepts Trump’s ambassadorial choice. Lula will face senator Flávio Bolsonaro , whose father once served as Brazil’s president and whose family has many ties with the Trump administration, in the 4 October polls. The administration has numerous issues with the leftist Lula and his policies and has also hosted the younger Bolsonaro, who is seeking to carry on his father, Jair’s, conservative governance. Joseph Gedeon reporting from Michigan: While outside a voting site in Dearborn, a confident Abdul El-Sayed not only believes he will win the primary, but has his sights set on Republican opponent Mike Rogers, predicting he “will beat [Rogers] by seven” in November. He called Rogers “generationally boring and generationally corrupt” adding that he “can’t decide what era of Republicanism he wants to be, so he carries the baggage of both.” “I’m hoping that that all of the senators who want to see a [Democratic] majority are going to team up, so we can all collectively dunk on Mike Rogers” he told reporters. The Trump administration is reportedly drafting a ban on US imports of new models of Chinese datacenter components, in the latest sign US authorities are scrambling to respond to the rapid development of AI technology in China. Four people familiar with the matter told Reuters that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which oversees the US ⁠telecommunications industry, is developing a measure to bar imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel over fiber-optic cables at the speed of light within datacenters. Officials hope to publish the measure this year, according to Reuters. The FCC could still modify or shelve the restriction, Reuters reported. But the deliberations are the latest example the Trump administration is increasingly focused on limiting Chinese technological incursions into cutting-edge US industries. An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. Levin added that those could include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses”, and requests for investigations by various government entities, including Congress. Hearn, 67, was arrested on 19 June and faced one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine – which he denied. Senate majority leader John Thune was asked about embattled House representative Max Miller, who is the ex-son-in-law of Republican senator Bernie Moreno. “It’s a family matter and, um, I don’t have any observations beyond that,” Thune said. When asked by a reporter about whether a member of Congress who is accused of domestic violence should continue to serve in their role, the Republican leader said: “It’s a House matter. It’s a family issue too.” The House ethics committee announced Tuesday it will launch an investigation into allegations that Max Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”. The announcement comes hours after the embattled Republican from Ohio said he had “nothing to hide” and welcomed the investigation. Senator Bernie Moreno told reporters that the dispute between his daughter, Emily Moreno, and her ex-husband, Representative Max Miller, has been “truly the seventh level of hell.” “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family,” the Ohio senator said. Senator Moreno feared what could happen to his granddaughter, especially after Miller’s attorney accidentally released a private image of Miller’s child in documents shared by the congressman. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for bein…

title: Jetstar to charge passengers up to $52 to put baggage in overhead lockers
summary: Airline says struggling to find room in overhead lockers on planes a ‘stressful part of the airport experience’
body: Jetstar will charge its passengers up to $52 to put carry-on baggage in the overhead locker, in a major change to the budget airline’s carry-on rules. In a press release on Wednesday morning, the airline announced it would remove the 7kg weight limit for carry-on bags, beginning in February 2027. There will still be size restrictions. The change follows extensive research and feedback from customers and crew who consistently identified having bags weighed at the gate and struggling to find room in overhead lockers as the more stressful parts of the airport experience, the airline said. “We know that weighing carry-on bags at the gate can be frustrating for our customers and for our crew,” the CEO of Jetstar, Stephanie Tully, said. Instead, all bookings will include one underseat bag such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag. Customers who need more carry-on baggage can pay a “Priority Carry-on” fee, which includes a second, larger bag for the overhead locker and the opportunity to be among the first to board. Prices depend on the flight: $25 for Launceston to Sydney, $33 Sydney to Melbourne, and up to $52 for Cairns to Tokyo. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The size-based carry-on baggage model is “similar to other leading low-fares carriers around the world”, the airline said. “From February, the main thing customers will need to think about is the size of their carry-on,” Tully said. “By giving customers an underseat bag with the option to add Priority Carry-on, we can make better use of overhead locker space, streamline boarding and help more flights depart on time. “Our new carry-on baggage model provides more choice to customers while helping to keep our fares low. You only pay for what you need – travelling with less means paying less, and you can always add more if you need.” Jetstar will no longer routinely use cabin baggage scales but will still ask customers to keep carry-on bags to 10kg so they can safely lift it themselves. Customers travelling with an infant will be able to take an extra underseat bag for their baby items, at no extra cost. The underseat bags can be up to 40 × 30 × 20cm and overhead bags can be up to 56 × 36 × 23cm. There are no changes to Jetstar’s checked baggage allowance, which remains purchasable for up to 40kg per passenger.

title: Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area
summary: Suspect had a prior conviction for reportedly shooting his father in Arizona, after he told his son to do the dishes
body: Authorities on Monday charged a man in Washington state with starting a wildfire that has consumed almost 4,000 acres and forced tens of thousands from their homes. Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for setting the Old Trails fire, the largest of three devastating wildfires burning through the region. He was found in possession of waterproof matches and a butane lighter – and was identified by witnesses who spotted him kneeling in grass close to where the blaze began over the weekend. At a press conference on Monday night, John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, said Farinacci had been apprehended quickly. “As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr Farinacci,” Nowels said. “This was fantastic, very quick work by everybody involved.” Nowels also offered details of the suspect, including that he had a prior conviction in Arizona for manslaughter. According to the Phoenix New Times, the victim was Farinacci’s father, who was shot and killed at their Mesa home in 2010, reportedly after telling his son to do the dishes. Farinacci was later found injured by a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Farinacci, then aged 21, pleaded guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. A judge found he was mentally fit to assist in his own defense, though defense lawyer Jose Colon continued to raise questions about his mental health and said that he had been hospitalized multiple times for psychiatric treatment, court records show. Beth Farinacci, who had married Aaron Farinacci’s father, said second-degree murder, not manslaughter, would have been a more appropriate way to resolve that case. “Manslaughter is for when someone accidentally kills another person. It is not for someone who intentionally points a loaded gun at their father and shoots him in his face and back,” she wrote in a letter to the judge. It was also reported that Aaron Farinacci had been contacted by police twice before during fire investigations. Spokane police responded to reports of several fires on 8 July 2025, near Farinacci’s apartment. The area near the Spokane River involved several “bus-sized” fires and prompted a significant emergency response, according to a police record. The Washington state patrol made contact with Farinacci the following month while pursuing a suspect in a wildfire at Riverside state park. They found him on a park bench, “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. They took photos of him. He was wearing a green T-shirt just like the one he was seen wearing on Saturday, the document says. Farinacci was expected to make his first court appearance Tuesday, Nowels said, as crews continued to battle the fires that have expanded across the county. The Old Trails fire started Saturday north-west of downtown Spokane. The blaze jumped the Spokane river and ripped through neighborhoods that some residents were able to return to on Monday. “There’s nothing to save,” said Miriam Sim, 76, as she and her husband, Daniel Sim, surveyed the ruined home where they had lived since 2005. In one Spokane neighborhood, blackened vehicles, a boat twisted by the heat and melted plastic recycling bins remained. Across the street, lawns were still green and houses were spared, as residents continued to run hoses or sprinklers to water their properties. More than 67,000 people were told to evacuate the three fires – Old Trail, Autumn Lane and Fairview – that by early Tuesday had burned about 16 sq miles (41 sq km) of Spokane, although orders in some areas were downgraded late on Monday. Elsewhere across the state, where extreme high temperatures and a fourth year of drought conditions have taken hold, there were at least 15 wildfires burning, covering at least 390 sq miles. Washington state’s entire congressional delegation wrote to Donald Trump on Monday urging the president to approve an expedited emergency declaration. Bob Ferguson, the state’s Democratic governor, said he spoke to the White House over the weekend after making his own emergency declaration. “Hundreds of people have completely lost their homes and farms, and many are prohibited from returning to their homes or neighborhoods as crews continue to extinguish smoldering embers,” the politicians’ letter said. No deaths or major injuries have been reported, although Cpl Mark Gregory, a spokesperson for the Spokane sheriff’s office, said Monday that 14 remained unaccounted for. They were, he said, probably people who had not been in contact since evacuating and were not truly missing or in danger. More than 1,000 firefighters, many from out of state, arrived by Monday to help tackle the blazes, a number expected to double in the coming days, authorities said. Crews continued to fight the fires by land and air, with Nowels warning the public during the Monday press conference not to interfere with aerial operations by using drones. A bulletin issued by the National Weather Service (NWS)’s Spokane office on Tuesday morning warned that challenging conditions would persist through the remainder of the week. “Extensive amounts of smoke will continue over the region, maintaining unhealthy air quality,” it said. “Dry conditions and breezy winds increase Friday and Saturday across portions of central Washington, bringing elevated fire weather conditions.” Hundreds of homes, businesses, and other structures have been destroyed in what Dave Upthegrove, Washington’s commissioner of public lands, called “an extraordinary wildfire season across the Pacific northwest”. The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: Jay Clayton sworn in as US director of national intelligence
summary: After a bumpy confirmation hearing, Clayton replaces acting director Bill Pulte to head US intelligence agencies
body: Jay Clayton has been sworn in as the US’s top spy after a contentious Senate confirmation hearing during which ⁠he refused to directly ⁠acknowledge that Donald Trump lost the 2020 presidential election. The oath of office was administered to Clayton on Tuesday by the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in the Oval Office as the president looked on and applauded. He becomes the ninth director of national intelligence, replacing Tulsi Gabbard, who stepped down in June. Clayton, a former US attorney for the southern district of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), will oversee 18 US intelligence agencies. His appointment follows a turbulent two months in which the intelligence apparatus was temporarily led by Bill Pulte, the housing regulator whom Trump installed as acting director after Gabbard’s departure. Pulte’s appointment had unsettled some Republicans because of his lack of national security experience. During his brief tenure, however, he became involved in the administration’s increasingly prominent campaign to raise concerns about the integrity of US elections. Shortly before Clayton’s confirmation, Pulte released intelligence community documents from 2020 describing China’s capacity to interfere in US politics and vulnerabilities in the election system. The material was largely previously known but its release came as Trump has made “election security” a central political issue ahead of November’s midterm elections. Trump has continued to promote false claims that the 2020 election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was stolen. During Pulte’s tenure, he also released classified material that he said supported his arguments. Clayton’s own confirmation was overshadowed by the same issue. Democrats condemned his refusal to state that Biden had won the election, while Republicans ultimately confirmed him along party lines. The controversy has raised questions about how the intelligence community will operate under a president who has repeatedly accused federal agencies of being “weaponised” against him. In his first statement as director, Clayton sought to address those concerns, promising to protect the intelligence community from political interference. “The safety and security of the ‌American people will be ‌our North Star, and we will work to make sure the ‌American people have complete confidence in the [intelligence community] through proper oversight, transparency and accountability,” Clayton said in a press release from the office of the director of national intelligence. “This includes ensuring the vital work of our [intelligence community] is never weaponized for political motives,” he added, echoing language frequently used by Trump and his allies to describe their claims that previous administrations abused federal power to target the president. Clayton brings substantial experience in law enforcement and government to the job. As US attorney in Manhattan, he oversaw prosecutions involving terrorism, international drug trafficking and organised crime. Before that, he chaired the SEC from 2017 to 2020, where the administration says he oversaw more than 2,300 enforcement actions resulting in more than $10bn in penalties and disgorgement. He has also held senior positions in business and law, including at Apollo Global Management and Sullivan & Cromwell, and has taught at the University of Pennsylvania and Wharton. Republican senators have pointed to that record as evidence that Clayton is qualified to lead the intelligence community. John Thune, the Senate majority leader, has called him a “proven leader” whose record inspired confidence. Tom Cotton, the chair of the Senate intelligence committee, said Clayton had deep experience in national security threats. Other Republican supporters highlighted his previous bipartisan confirmation as SEC chair. Senator Katie Britt of Alabama added via X on Tuesday: “Congratulations to our Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton! I look forward to seeing him lead our intelligence community and keep our nation safe from threats.” Clayton now inherits an intelligence community that has already endured a succession of upheavals under Trump. Gabbard’s tenure was marked by clashes with congressional Democrats, who accused her of advancing the president’s political agenda and promoting debunked election claims. Pulte’s temporary appointment then raised fresh concerns about the politicisation of the intelligence agencies. Clayton said his aim was to create an intelligence organisation that was “streamlined, agile, team-oriented and mission-focused”. He added: “I look forward to making sure the men and women of the [intelligence community] have the resources they need to carry out our critical mission.” With just more than three months left before midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, Trump has escalated efforts ‌to make “election security” a central issue, despite established findings that voter fraud is rare.

title: New York deputy police commissioner fired after attempted murder arrest
summary: Mount Vernon official is accused of driving getaway car after son allegedly opened fire outside Bronx court
body: A New York state police department fired its deputy commissioner on Tuesday after she allegedly acted as a getaway driver for her son in what is being investigated as an attempted murder. The city of Mount Vernon said in an Instagram post that it had terminated Jennifer Lackard, deputy police commissioner for safety, for conduct “unrelated to her duties”. Lackard, 49, and her 20-year-old son Chase were arrested in an early morning raid on Tuesday at their home in New York City’s Bronx borough, according to the New York Daily News, citing “police sources”. The newspaper said the pair were charged with attempted murder, attempted assault, gun possession, conspiracy and reckless endangerment, in connection with shots that were fired at a group of people outside Bronx criminal court on 29 June. Chase Lackard was the alleged gunman, according to the Daily News – and jumped into a car that was driven from the scene at speed by his mother. Nobody was struck or injured during the shooting. The Mount Vernon statement referenced the charges against Lackard in its announcement of her firing. The announcement described her as the city’s former deputy police commissioner of wellness. “The Mount Vernon police department is aware of the criminal charges filed by the Bronx county district attorney’s office against former deputy commissioner of wellness, Jennifer Lackard,” the statement said. “Effective immediately, the city of Mount Vernon has terminated Jennifer Lackard’s employment. The allegations are unrelated to her duties with the Mount Vernon [police] and do not stem from any conduct associated with the department or the performance of her official responsibilities.” According to the See Through NY government transparency website, Lackard’s salary was $138,219 in 2025. Chase Lackard had previously been shot multiple times, according to reports. In January 2023, when he was 17, he was reportedly shot in the chest on a bus in a reported dispute over gang signs with three other boys. A 14-year-old member of a rival gang was later arrested and charged with attempted murder. At the time, Mount Vernor mayor Shawyn Patterson-Howard called Jennifer Lackard “a valuable member of our leadership team” – and said the city was praying for her son’s recovery. Then, in November 2024, police in the Bronx responded to reports of a large fight and ended up shooting Chase Lackard, then 19, after he was alleged to have pointed a 9mm pistol at an officer’s car. Lackard was taken to hospital with two gunshot wounds to a leg and later criminally charged. The New York City police department’s chief of patrol, John Chell, told reporters that Lackard was also arrested in September 2024 on a gun charge. In a statement following that episode, the Mount Vernon mayor called it “a personal matter and we are praying for the family”. No lawyer was immediately listed for Lackards on Tuesday. The city of Mount Vernon said it “will not comment on the underlying allegations”. The Guardian sent a request for comment to the Bronx county district attorney’s office.

title: Washington state Democrat who flipped pro-Trump district faces tough primary
summary: Incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a moderate who owns an auto repair shop, hopes to retain congressional seat
body: The two-term Democratic congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is heading into one of the country’s most closely watched contests on Tuesday after national recognition for flipping a Republican seat in 2022. Representing Washington state’s third district, Gluesenkamp Perez finds herself squeezed between Democrat and progressive Brent Hennrich and Republican state senator John Braun on her right. There are six other candidates on a single crowded ballot and the top two finishers will advance to the November general election regardless of party. Democrats are favored to win the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election, but highly contested seats such as Gluesenkamp Perez’s will be crucial to securing a majority, and expanding the margin. Republican Jaime Herrera Beutler won Washington’s third district in 2010 and held it for six terms, until Gluesenkamp Perez narrowly beat Trump-endorsed Joe Kent in 2022. Trump has carried the district in all three of his presidential runs, most recently by about three points, and yet in 2024 Gluesenkamp Perez ran roughly seven points ahead of her party’s presidential nominee. Logging, mills, agriculture, shipping and manufacturing still shape daily life in much of the area and Gluesenkamp Perez’s success has stemmed from her appeal to moderates and rural voters. An auto repair shop owner, she won over many in south-west Washington, including Republicans who considered Kent too extreme. “We like her a lot,” said Laura Oltmann, 41, a resident and supporter who describes herself as a conservative. Kent did not embody conservatism, Oltmann said. But through Gluesenkamp Perez’s two terms, frustration has built among her own party, growing when Democrats saw her siding with Republicans on major legislation. Hennrich, who is challenging her in the primary, ran for the same seat in 2022 before standing down, but decided to run again. “I stepped out of this race to unify Democrats to help get Marie through, so we could get rid of our six-term incumbent, Jaime Herrera Beutler,” he said. “[Gluesenkamp Perez] has turned out to be just an absolute epic failure for Democrats.” Hennrich is not alone. Several local Democratic organizations inside the district have broken with her. “She ran as a Democrat and inspired a lot of people, and she won, and we thought she was going to be what we wanted her to be. But everybody’s disappointed,” said LaDonna Kirkpatrick, chair of the 18th Legislative District Democrats, speaking in a personal capacity. Kirkpatrick traces that disappointment to Gluesenkamp Perez’s votes for the Save Act, Trump’s effort to overhaul elections, as well as for a bill restricting how public schools address gender identity, and federal funding tied to the war in Iran. She claims the congresswoman has also stopped talking to her own party’s local officers. Thea Zahn, the chair of the 20th legislative district, agreed. “What majority are you going for?” she said. “Are you going for a majority that believes in Democratic values, or a majority that will fail over and over again when it comes down to it, when you really need people to stand up and say this is what we believe in?” Asked if she would vote for the congresswoman if she is on the ballot in November, Zahn said: “I won’t vote for Marie. I will never vote for Marie Perez again.” The congresswoman’s defenders make a different argument: that the district’s partisan lean leaves her little room, and that the seat matters more than any single vote. “The reality is we live in a Republican district. It is Republican,” said Terri Niles, who chairs the 17th Legislative District Democrats and spoke in a personal capacity. “I’ve knocked on tens of thousands of doors.” Niles argues that none of Gluesenkamp Perez’s contentious votes actually resulted in legislation passing, and that the calculation for Democrats is simpler than her critics allow. “The most important thing everybody should keep in mind is that flipping the House is our goal,” she said. “That should be the most important thing for every Democrat out there.” The Democratic infighting comes at a precarious moment. An Emerson College poll conducted in mid-July for the Northwest Progressive Institute found Gluesenkamp Perez and Republican Braun tied. Braun, the Republican leader in the Washington senate, has become one of the GOP’s top congressional recruits, earning Donald Trump’s endorsement in April and the backing of the National Republican Congressional Committee. “We could hand a truly 100% Maga candidate a congressional seat for life,” said Tim Probst, a local Democratic party leader. “Because once he gets in there, he’s not getting out.”

title: University of Maryland ‘teacher of the year’ detained by ICE in Texas
summary: DHS said pharmacy instructor Berhanu Kibret overstayed visa and arrested him at Dallas-Fort Worth airport
body: An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location. In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award. “Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS. Kibret’s research focuses on how the brain’s cannabinoid system influences mental health, brain disease and the effects of addictive drugs, the university’s website says. He obtained bachelor’s and master’s degrees in science as well as a PhD in Ethiopia – and he completed his postdoctoral fellowship at William Paterson University in Wayne, New Jersey. Calling Kibret a “highly valued member of the University of Maryland, Baltimore community”, the school said it was “greatly troubled” by his arrest. The university added: “He is an effective and beloved teacher, and a highly regarded colleague. His detention has generated not only great sympathy for his plight, but also a heightened sense of apprehension here on campus.” In a statement to the Guardian, the DHS said ICE arrested Kibret after he entered the US on 21 June 2021 on a visa set to expire on 31 May 2024. “Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his visa and failed to depart,” the DHS statement said. “He will remain in ICE custody pending his immigration proceedings.” The Guardian has reached out to the University of Maryland, Baltimore for additional comment. Arrests such as that of Kibret have drawn criticism, particularly in light of the Trump administration’s repeated pledge to focus on targeting the “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” for arrest and deportation. A Guardian analysis published in February found that 77% of people placed into deportation proceedings for the first time after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 had no criminal convictions. Kibret’s arrest came after ICE in July detained and later released a Johns Hopkins researcher at the Baltimore/Washington international airport. Federal authorities detained Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian citizen with a doctorate in pharmacy who works at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health. Speaking to several outlets during Ameaka’s detention, a Johns Hopkins spokesperson described her as a “respected member of our community”. “The university understands the fear and concern this instills in members of our community,” the spokesperson added. “Dr Ameaka was traveling in a personal capacity, and though we cannot comment on the specifics of her situation, we want to assure our community that the university is actively working to provide support for Dr Ameaka, including ensuring she has access to legal representation.” Documents reviewed by ABC indicated that Ameaka held a work authorization valid through 2029 and had a pending asylum case. Nonetheless, as ABC reported, the DHS had initially said of Ameaka: “In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” Ameaka’s attorney on Sunday confirmed that she had been released from ICE detention. • This article was amended on 4 August 2026. An earlier version featured an image of University of Maryland, Baltimore County, rather than University of Maryland, Baltimore.

title: Ex-Olympian weighing ‘all options’ after reflecting pool charges dropped
summary: David Hearn has a ‘number of potential remedies’ after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage, his attorney says
body: An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. Levin added that those could include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions, and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses”, and requests for investigations by various government entities, including Congress. Hearn, 67, was arrested on 19 June and faced one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine – which he denied. The charge came after the Trump administration spent $14m to change the reflecting pool’s color. A new pool liner almost immediately began to peel off, and the president blamed vandals. Four people were arrested, but only Hearn was charged with a felony. On Friday, Trump’s justice department moved to dismiss the charge against Hearn, saying in a filing that the damage to the pool liner was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor” who worked on it. In a 20-page court filing in Washington DC superior court on Friday, prosecutors said they had received information about a “rush to complete the project” prior to events associated with the celebration of the US’s semiquincentennial on the Fourth of July. Washington DC’s US attorney, Jeanine Pirro, said that her office – which handles cases in the city’s superior court – had received key documents from the federal department of the interior after the indictment was filed. Those documents “indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the reflecting pool”, Pirro wrote in Friday’s court filing. The resulting decision to drop the charge against Hearn set off a dispute within the Trump administration. The president said Pirro had “choked” and “folded like an umbrella”, leading to speculation that she might be fired from her post. Donald Trump has continued to blame vandalism for problems with the pool makeover. On Monday, the president ducked questions about Pirro’s charge dismissal but maintained his criticism of her, saying: “I disagree 100% with [her].” Pirro was spotted at the White House hours after Trump’s comments on Monday. Attorneys for Hearn have previously said the government “owes Mr Hearn an apology”. “The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” his attorneys, including Levin, said on social media. “Its dismissal … does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong.” Hearn told the Associated Press that he had been detained by the national guard and US park police for five hours after stopping by the reflecting pool during a bike ride. He acknowledged that he briefly touched a part on the liner attached to the side and told NBC News the pool’s condition “was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there”. Lawyers for Hearn have also called on prosecutors to disclose the legal instructions they gave to grand jurors about the elements of the criminal charge handed up against him. “The grand jury transcripts disclosed to the defense thus far contain other irregularities that reflect a misleading presentation to the grand jury and a need for review of the entire grand jury record in this matter,” Hearn’s attorneys wrote. Hearn’s opportunities for legal recourse against the federal government may come only after his attorneys petition the court to dismiss the case “with prejudice”, meaning that it could not be refiled. The justice department dropped the charge “without prejudice”, meaning that it can be refiled. “We are responding with our own motion to dismiss with prejudice so that he is not longer at risk of being harassed by the government further,” Levin said on Tuesday. “Once that is resolved Mr Hearn will focus on what comes next. “He’s considering all options.” In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen said the team plans to go on the offensive against the government: “All legal remedies are on the table going forward to respond to the miscarriage of justice,” Eisen said.

title: Ohio Republican Max Miller faces growing calls to resign over domestic abuse allegations
summary: Miller vows to clear his name as Republican senator Bernie Moreno says former son-in-law unfit to serve in Congress
body: Max Miller, a US Republican representative from Ohio, is facing a rising groundswell of resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations after his ex-father-in-law, Bernie Moreno, a GOP senator, said he was unfit to serve in Congress. With a deadline looming for party leaders to choose a potential replacement, Miller, a former White House aide, also came under pressure from Donald Trump on Monday after the president reportedly called and told him “things aren’t looking good” for his re-election campaign against his Democratic opponent, Brian Poindexter. The congressional ethics committee launched an investigation into allegations that Miller “may have engaged in domestic violence and abuse or illegal drug use in violation of the code of official conduct or any other applicable standard of conduct”, it said on Tuesday. Earlier in the day, Miller said he would request an ethics investigation into himself “to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family”, adding: “I have absolutely nothing to hide.” Pleas for Miller to step down intensified after Moreno – the father of Miller’s former wife, Emily Moreno – broke his silence after months of refraining from comment on allegations concerning the alleged abuse of his daughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Moreno, an ally of Trump, posted on Sunday. “He should not serve in the House of Representatives.” Addressing reporters on Tuesday, Moreno described the dispute between his daughter and Miller as “truly the seventh level of hell”, adding: “This has been a horrific experience for my entire family. “This has been brutal beyond comprehension, and if there’s any minimum standard for being an elected official, as I said, he fails to meet that minimum basic standard,” the senator said. Moreno said he had to handle the pickup of his granddaughter at a police station this weekend because he didn’t “want my daughter interacting with this man”. “I don’t know what this guy’s capable of,” he said. Moreno’s comments came after Miller posted a livestream video defending himself against the abuse accusations and saying his former wife had “significant mental-health challenges”. A series of public statements from Moreno’s fellow Republican senators indicate that their sympathies are with him. “[Miller] should resign. He should quit,” Roger Marshall, a senator from Kansas, told Politico. “I don’t know Mr Miller’s story, but I trust Bernie [Moreno] so much as a good friend, and his family has such high values.” The West Virginia senator Shelley Moore Capito said: “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that.” Lisa Murkowski, a Republican senator from Alaska, said: “The accusations are very serious, and if there is truth to them, I am one who says that our elected officials need to be held to high standards. “And certainly, when it comes to allegations of domestic abuse, child abuse, that’s not what we want in our lawmakers.” Three other senators, Rick Scott of Florida, West Virginia’s Jim Justice and Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, also gave public backing to Moreno against Miller. “I don’t know enough about the allegations, but like Bernie said, it sounds like he thinks he needs psychological help,” said Scott. “I trust Bernie.” Miller – who married Emily Moreno at Trump’s club in Bedminster, New Jersey, in 2022 – has been accused of holding a gun to her head and scalding her with boiling water. Their toddler daughter, who was born in 2023, is also said to have suffered a broken collarbone due to his actions. Miller denies allegations of abuse and has filed a defamation case against his wife over the claims. The couple divorced in 2025. Axios reported that Trump called Miller on Monday amid concerns that the situation threatened Republican chances of holding the congressional seat in November’s midterms, when the party already faces an uphill challenge to keep its wafer-thin majority in the House of Representatives. But the president avoided taking sides when asked about the issue by reporters in the White House. “I know Max, he’s a good person. I mean, I always thought he was a very good person. And I’m going to let the families figure that out,” he said. Miller has resisted calls for him to withdraw from the race and told the Wall Street Journal that Trump “was supportive of me over the phone” on Monday’s call. “He said he had a poll with no detail, and I pushed back with our poll that has us winning by 9 with our message out there,” Miller told the newspaper. “He kept on reiterating it’s going to be tough, and it’s going to be a really hard one for you.” If Miller were to remove his name from the ballot before the close of business on Tuesday, a special Republican primary would be held to replace him. If he were to withdraw after that, the party would still need to replace him by 10 August, but would need to give two days notice beforehand to hold a meeting to choose a substitute candidate. • In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: Iran’s president denies threatening to resign during talks over strait of Hormuz
summary: Masoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’
body: Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been forced to deny claims that he has repeatedly threatened to resign as he battles hardline factions opposed to reaching a settlement with the US over the strait of Hormuz. The US and Europe hope a deal is imminent to reopen the strait and they are putting pressure on Oman to accept a temporary agreement that officials in Muscat fear will leave Iran retaining near permanent dominance of the vital oil shipping channel. Ships would enter the strait in a route close to Iran, but leave on a route that passes through Iranian and Omani waters. But far from being feted over an imminent diplomatic victory, Pezeshkian was instead forced to deny that he had repeatedly offered to resign, verbally and in writing, during a television interview marking his second anniversary in the job. Pezeshkian accused some of wishing to create a rift inside Iran and said: “If I want to resign, I will officially announce that I have resigned. I will not resign, I will stand.” The resignation claims, which have been front page news in Iran, were made by Mohammad Bagher Kharazi, who is linked by marriage to Mojtaba Khamenei, the new supreme leader. He said Pezeshkian had become frustrated at being excluded from decision making, made worse by the supreme leader’s reluctance to reveal his whereabouts for fear of foreign intelligence agencies. Khamenei was badly injured in the Israeli bombing on the first day of the war that killed his father and has not been seen or heard in public since. Kharazi claimed Pezeshkian had threatened to quit so many times that Khamenei warned him he would accept the next resignation threat, a claim Khamenei’s office eventually said on Tuesday was “fundamentally false and untrue”. Pezeshkian insisted in the interview that he was in complete harmony with the military and said those that claimed 30,000 people had been killed in the January protests never took up the offer to provide proof. The interview, marking the halfway point of his turbulent presidency, appeared to be an attempt to dispel the impression that his belief in consensus was a weakness, or that he had been sidelined by hardline war leaders. Kharazi is the brother-in-law of Massoud Khamenei, the younger brother of the supreme leader. Critics say he has a record of making unsubstantiated allegations and despite his family connections to the supreme leader, it is not clear if he has seen him since his elevation to the post in March. However, the row has highlighted the deep strategic and tactical differences inside Iran over the wisdom of talks with the US. Mehdi Tabatabaei, a senior member of the Iranian president’s office, described the reports as “complete nonsense and lies”. In a post on social media, he condemned a “sinister coalition of lying, deceitful and reckless extremism”whose members could not accept democratic outcomes. He said: “Two years have passed since their failure in the arena of national elections, yet they are still seeking revenge against the will of the nation. They have become puppets of Iran’s enemies.” Ahmad Zeidabadi, a reformist reporter, said the claims were inflammatory and served only to exacerbate tensions. Pezeshkian on Sunday suggested that the memorandum of understanding, negotiated with the US in June and reviled by some hardliners, would serve as a cornerstone for Iranian foreign relations in the future, saying that Iran “must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed”. On Monday, the conservative-dominated Assembly of Experts issued a statement describing hopes for an agreement or understanding with the US as “futile” and labelled what it termed “whispers of capitulation in the name of defending peace” an “unforgivable betrayal”. It added that trusting this arrogant government was nothing more than a mirage. Khamenei himself had said in April he was opposed to talks with the US in principle, but in deference to Pezeshkian had allowed them to go ahead.

title: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests
summary: Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
body: India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government. Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar. The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks that forced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure. Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs. The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state. Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment. Deepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.” The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of Working India report by Azim Premji University. The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined. The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign. After he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds. A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests. The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook. The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content. The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status. “The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said. Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.” But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”

title: BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to Burnham
summary: Meg O’Neill is overseeing rapid clearing of the decks at BP after strategic muddle of recent years, with ‘message’ for new PM
body: BP will ignore “sentiment” and “history” in pruning its portfolio of assets, says its new-ish boss, Meg O’Neill. She demonstrated as much last week when putting the company’s 60-year-old North Sea oil and gas business up for sale, explaining on Tuesday that “it just doesn’t compete” in the internal battle for capital. Now comes a disposal that sends an equally unsentimental message about priorities. The US biogas business, Archaea, which was a prized acquisition in the brief green-tinged era of Bernard Looney, is on the block less than four years after BP bought it for $4bn (£2.98bn). Back in 2022, Looney, O’Neill’s predecessor-but-one, cooed over Archaea, which taps methane from landfill sites. It was “a fantastic fast-growing business” that would add “distinctive value” and “support our net zero ambition”. One hefty write-down later, the operation is judged surplus to requirements because it’s too capital-hungry for a group in debt-reduction mode. The clearing of the decks at BP is happening quickly after the strategic muddle of recent years. A sale of the solar power unit Lightsource is close but, as with the North Sea assets, it’s not just the green assets that are a target. A major refinery in Gelsenkirchen in Germany has gone. So, too, the Austrian fuel stations. And the sale of the lubricants business Castrol was under way before O’Neill arrived. By the end of the year, reckons BP, it will have reached its target to get net debt below $18bn, 12 months ahead of schedule. The process will have been massively assisted, of course, by the boom in profits and cashflow that followed the surge in oil and gas profits with the Iran war. BP’s profits more than doubled to $5.73bn in the three months to the end of June. Cue understandable outrage among campaign groups but zero surprise on the part of City analysts. BP sold its oil at an average of $94 a barrel in the second quarter, up from $67 in the first, enjoying only a slightly smaller increase in the price of natural gas. Profits were obviously going to be enormous, just as they have been at other oil majors. That is doubly so when constraints in the global flow of oil meant refining the stuff – where BP is also big – became a licence to print money in the period. For O’Neill, the next question from investors will be when she is going to rejoin other majors and restart share buy-backs, which were cancelled in February when the strain on the balance sheet was more acute than it is now. She dodged the question on Tuesday – but shareholders will expect an answer from a straight-talking chief executive soon-ish. Still, she was clear in the advice she had given to Andy Burnham if the new prime minister wished, as he says he does, to take a “pragmatic” approach to the North Sea. “The message I left him with was: the UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas,” O’Neill said. “The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts.” That is the case for more (or just more stable) domestic volumes, even as the UK keeps decarbonising: you do it to minimise imports, particularly of liquefied natural gas with its higher associated emissions. The UK’s net import dependency was 43.5% in 2025. There’s no chance of O’Neill reversing BP’s exit from the North Sea, it seems, but the other implied message in her comments about the competitiveness of the basin wasn’t hard to grasp. If Burnham wants to boost domestic supplies, it won’t be enough just to approve Adura’s Jackdaw and Rosebank fields for production. There will also have to be a rethink on the energy profits levy, AKA the windfall tax that dates from 2022, to incentivise investment. Politically speaking, it is tricky to lower the level at which windfall rates apply at a moment when the Iran war has created a fresh corporate profits bonanza globally. Burnham has said he was “looking at” the levy. It is one of the unavoidable big choices for October’s budget.

title: BP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North Sea
summary: Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double
body: BP’s chief executive has urged Andy Burnham to make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even as the oil company prepares to sell its North Sea business after 60 years in the ageing basin. In a conversation with the new prime minister, Meg O’Neill said the country should prioritise using energy produced in the UK, “where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts”. BP’s endorsement of UK oil production came days after the 117-year-old company signalled a plan to exit the North Sea after six decades, as part of a wider plan to streamline its business. O’Neill said North Sea investments were “not competitive” within BP’s portfolio, while the company reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine because of rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis. BP’s quarterly profits more than doubled to $5.73bn (£4.27bn) in the three months to the end of June, as the conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt energy exports from the Gulf. O’Neill added that BP had already received several unsolicited approaches to buy its North Sea fields and she was “very optimistic” that the assets would “continue to be profitable in the hands of a future owner”. Burnham’s government is expected to make a decision on whether to allow two controversial North Sea oil and gas projects – the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields – to move ahead despite growing outrage over oil company profits and evidence of a deepening global climate crisis. The new ministers are also facing calls to reform the North Sea tax regime. The industry has consistently argued that the UK government’s high taxes on oil and gas accelerate its natural decline. In an interview with CNBC News, O’Neill said Burnham had “reinforced his desire to work closely with business” and “be pragmatic”. She said: “The UK gets 75% of its energy from fossil fuels today, so that’s oil and natural gas. The first barrel of oil we consume and molecule of natural gas we need should be coming from the UK North Sea, where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts. “The UK is still using a huge amount of oil and natural gas every single day, and we ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party. “You know, I think the new prime minister has come in with a focus on being pragmatic, and with a focus on understanding how communities around the nation can benefit from developing local economic outcomes.” Burnham was warned last week he could face the first revolt of his premiership over his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas. BP revealed its climbing profits days after Shell posted its second highest quarterly earnings on record after months of market volatility caused by the Middle East crisis. Europe’s largest oil company doubled its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June, the highest since its record earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Middle East crisis has helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in net profits to $32.69bn in the three months ending on 30 June, despite disruption in ‌the strait of Hormuz, owing to higher sales revenue for refined and chemical products and crude oil. The windfall profits for the world’s biggest oil and gas companies have faced criticism. Households and businesses are struggling with rising energy bills, and millions have been affected by severe heatwaves across Europe, which are made more likely and more severe by the fossil fuel-driven climate crisis. Donald Trump has said Chevron and ExxonMobil, which also reported sharp profit increases this week, are “making too much money” and should return some of their profits to the public. Rosie Downes, the head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “Clearly not everyone is feeling the pain of the energy crisis. While BP banks another round of enormous profits, millions of households are paying the price through sky-high energy bills and a climate crisis accelerating rapidly out of control with increasingly severe heatwaves, wildfires and droughts.”
